title: Body-Self Relations, Eating Behaviors, and Occupational Factors Associated with BMI and Obesity in Mass Catering Workers: A Cross-Sectional Study
content: Background: Mass catering workers combine repeated food exposure with occupational demands, yet evidence integrating eating behavior, body-self relations, and work characteristics is limited. Methods: This cross-sectional study included 452 mass catering workers in Isparta, Türkiye. BMI was calculated from measured weight and height. Body-self relations, eating behaviors, and occupational characteristics were assessed using the MBSRQ, TFEQ-R18, and Swedish Demand-Control-Support Questionnaire. BMI-group comparisons, Spearman correlations, and multivariable linear regression with HC3 robust standard errors were performed; obesity models were secondary. Results: Mean BMI was 28.38 ± 4.66 kg/m2; 31.4% had overweight and 44.2% had obesity. Body-self relation scores decreased and uncontrolled eating increased across BMI groups (both adjusted p&lt;0.001). BMI correlated negatively with body-self relations (ρ=-0.465) and positively with uncontrolled eating (ρ=0.427). In the fully adjusted model, higher body-self relations were associated with lower BMI (β=-2.816, 95% CI -3.855 to -1.778), whereas uncontrolled eating was associated with higher BMI (β=0.0347 per point, 95% CI 0.0190 to 0.0503). Conclusions: Higher BMI was consistently associated with less favorable body-self relations and greater uncontrolled eating, supporting their consideration in occupational weight-management research.
